analysis.one_liner: Requires all commercial trucks to have automatic emergency braking systems.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Department of Transportation to write a safety rule requiring every commercial motor vehicle to carry a forward collision avoidance and braking system — equipment that warns the driver of an obstacle ahead and automatically applies the brakes if a crash is imminent [S2] [S3]. It gave the Secretary one year to write the standard and required compliance on all commercial vehicles within three years of enactment [S3]. The bill never advanced past its initial committee referrals [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who shares the road with large trucks — passenger-car occupants, pedestrians, cyclists, and truck drivers themselves — because automatic emergency braking is designed to prevent rear-end and obstacle collisions before they happen [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Transportation Secretary to set a federal safety standard mandating that commercial motor vehicles be equipped with systems that alert drivers to obstacles and automatically brake to avoid or reduce the severity of a collision [S2] [S3].
Sets a firm deadline: all commercial vehicles must carry the equipment no later than three years after enactment, rather than leaving adoption voluntary [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Motor carriers — the trucking and bus companies that own commercial vehicles — would bear the cost of purchasing and installing the braking systems across their fleets, and those costs could be passed to shippers and consumers in freight prices [S3].

drawbacks.text: The mandate imposes an unfunded equipment requirement on commercial fleets, including small trucking operators, and compliance within three years could be costly for older vehicles still in service [S3].

The bill sets a compliance deadline without funding, studies, or phase-in flexibility; opponents of such mandates typically argue that the technology should be adopted as it matures rather than by fixed statutory date.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Automatic emergency braking is a proven crash-avoidance technology, and large trucks cause disproportionate harm in collisions because of their mass, so the safety benefit to the public is large relative to an equipment cost that fleets routinely absorb for other mandated safety gear. The bill's main design weakness is its rigid three-year deadline rather than its goal.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and their subcommittees, and no committee ever voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Hank Johnson introduced the bill on September 17, 2015, joined by Reps. David Scott and John Lewis of Georgia, with two cosponsors [S3] [S4] [S5].

It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee, then to the Highways and Transit and the Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade subcommittees on September 18, 2015 [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill sat in committee without a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote until the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commercial fleet owners are better off because the bill died: they avoided a federal requirement to buy and install automatic emergency braking on every commercial vehicle. The cost of preventable truck collisions — borne by crash victims and their families — remained where it was.

for.name: Rep. Henry C. "Hank" Johnson Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Safe Roads Act to require automatic emergency braking on commercial motor vehicles.

for.name: Reps. David Scott and John Lewis
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill's introduction; it drew two cosponsors in total.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters were House Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the bill died in committee with no recorded opposition votes, so the partisan split is one of sponsorship rather than a roll call.

industries.note: The bill would have required fleets to equip every commercial vehicle with automatic emergency braking within three years, a real capital cost — falling hardest on small operators — in exchange for fewer crashes involving their vehicles. Fleet safety costs in crashes are externalized to the public, so the industry's interest in avoiding the mandate ran against public safety.

industries.industry: Collision-avoidance and vehicle safety equipment makers
industries.note: A federal mandate would have created a guaranteed market for the sensor and braking systems, and the industry's gain coincides with more protected road users.
